newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro stocks take Greenspan warning in their stride.
newsitem.headline: Euro stocks take Greenspan warning in their stride.

text.p: European stock markets are taking in their stride a warning from U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on share valuations and analysts said on Thursday European bourses are in less risk of falling than Wall Street.

Investors have factored in U.S. monetary tightening through a rate rise and such a hike would further bolster the dollar, making European stocks an attractive buy for investors looking to cash in on the benefit to European exports.

"There is far less downside risk in Europe than on Wall Street because there is enough money waiting to buy when shares come down," said market analyst Gary Dugan at J.P. Morgan in London, who expects a 0.25 percent point rise in U.S. rates.
The pool of money available to invest could become even bigger if U.S. funds switched to Europe and expecially if bond investors sold government paper to buy equities.
"I would expect some switching from U.S. funds to the continent, especially France," said a Paris trader.

Greenspan on Wednesday cautioned in his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress that a two-year rise in U.S. equities was perhaps not sustainable and he said the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates even before there were signs of inflation picking up.
Wall Street's Dow Jones stock index closed 55 points down on Wednesday, after having been down by more than 110, but European share markets on Thursday resumed their rise.

Expected increases in company profits and economic growth are driving share markets higher. A key factor in this is the level of the dollar, whose recent rise boosted European stocks as a higher U.S. currency helps European exports -- and export-driven growth which could create jobs in Europe.
"The dollar is the most important factor right now driving the market and that has a heavier impact than Greenspan," said a trader at a Munich bank.

In Germany, the DAX index, which measures floor trade in 30 German blue-chips, is close to its life high of 3,287.79 points. In France, the CAC-40 blue-chip index was also within spitting distance of its all-time high of 2,658.62 -- set on February 18 -- and analysts expect a test of the level soon.
London stocks were trading off highs on Thursday afternoon as investors shook off the Greenspan remarks and focused on a Parliamentary local election.
The Amsterdam market has also been boosted by fresh liquidity and is steering its own course, independently from Greenspan.

The high inflow is, however, somewhat artificial because of very low interest rates and a new kind of investment fund. A slew of strong 1996 year results from leading companies and expectation of more such figures have also buoyed the market.

Inflation worries are limited in the Netherlands, partly because the German economy is in a difficult position, although some dealers anticipate a small interest rate rise, which could depress the market. Most analysts expect the main Dutch AEX index to rise to 800 points in the short-term, from 750 today.

In Stockholm, Swedish share prices were boosted by strong capital flows onto the market. "A lot of money keeps coming into the market," said Anders Bruzelius, analyst at Handelsbanken. "In January, there were extremely high amounts placed in equity funds," he added.
In Milan, however, the Italian stock market lost slightly more than two percent on Wednesday and more on Thursday with analysts saying it had been in need of a correction.
"Milan tends to accentuate the falls on Wall Street," said Alberto Rolla, equity analyst at brokers Pasfin.

"It's an emotionally driven market, latin and in a marginal position in respect to the bigger markets. People buy less when foreign bourses are positive and they sell more in the opposite case," Rolla said.
